div.p: Dear Pound: Walsh wrote that T.Q . had been transferred to Milan where it was being printed, that you were in Milan and that he was going there to see you in ten days. He suggested that, if I was in the clinic, you might correct my proofs. Of course I would not think of inflicting that on you but I thought you were managing or editing the review there. It seems you are in Rapallo . I hope they send me the proofs in time. Did I tell you Exiles is to be given by the Stage Society ?

div.note: This postcard, in JJ’s hand, is misaddressed to Pound at “19 via Marsala / Rapallo / (Italie).” The Pounds had a flat at 12 via Marsala (see JJ to Pound, 31 December 1924, notes). The face of the postcard shows a photograph of a beach and pier crowded with tourists and bathers, and is captioned: “67. – Arcachon (Gironde). – La Grande Jetée, la Plage et le Grand-Hôtel. M.D.” The photograph is credited to “Marcel Delboy, Bordeaux.” Jacques Marcel Delboy (1903-1941) was a French photographer who published his images on black-and-white collotype postcards and in souvenir booklets. His work was often signed “M.D.,” “Delboy,” or “Yobled.”

This Quarter was a review devoted to experimental literature, art, and music, edited by the American poet Ernest Walsh (1895-1926) and the Scottish suffragist Ethel Moorhead (1869-1955). They produced the first issue from Paris, then moved their headquarters to Milan so that Walsh, who suffered from tuberculosis, could benefit from the warmer climate (for a fuller account of the editors and the review, see JJ to Pound, 23 August 1925, notes). Walsh visited Pound, evidently in Rapallo, Italy, in early September 1925 (Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 575).
JJ had had eye surgery, his eighth operation, in April 1925, and was facing additional surgery in the coming months (see JJ to Pound, 23 August 1925, notes).

A portion of JJ’s “Work in Progress” was published in This Quarter (Milan), vol. 1, no. 2 (Autumn-Winter 1925-1926): 108-123. This portion would become what is known as the Shem chapter, Book I, Chapter 7, of Finnegans Wake (1939), pages 169-95 (for further details, see JJ to Pound, 23 August 1925, notes).

Pound had been offering informal advice to This Quarter, but, as he wrote the editor of the Paris Chicago Tribune in early September 1925, he had “no editorial connection with any current periodical” at this time (Chicago Tribune [Paris] [3 September 1925]: 4). For further details, see JJ to Pound, 23 August 1925, notes.

Since early 1925, Pound and his wife Dorothy, née Shakespear (1886-1973), had been living in a top-floor apartment at 12 via Marsala in the northern Italian town of Rapallo, about 15 miles from Genoa and just over 100 miles from Milan. For details of Pound’s move from Paris to Italy, see JJ to Pound, 31 December 1924, notes.

Founded in 1899, the London-based Incorporated Stage Society presented new, experimental, and sometimes controversial plays, including those by George Bernard Shaw, W.B. Yeats, Henrik Ibsen, and Gerhart Hauptmann. Shaw, J.M. Barrie, and others were officials of the company, which staged private performances of plays that had been denied a license for public performance by the Lord Chamberlain. The Society considered Exiles during 1916 and 1917 but in the end did not mount it, possibly because of disagreement over certain “tabooed” words, as Shaw later suggested (Ellmann, JJ 443 n.). The Society finally presented Exiles at London’s Regent Theatre on 14 and 15 February 1926, with W.G. Fay as director. “The house was nearly full,” Ellmann notes, “and the audience was laudatory, especially for the first two acts, the third puzzling them perhaps by its ambiguous ending (Ellmann, JJ 575). Exiles had received its first performance in Munich (translated into German as Verbannte) on 7 August 1919.
